# Introduction to Amos

## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of Amos

1. Amos introduced (1:1)
2. Yahweh judges the surrounding nations (1:2–2:3), the southern kingdom of Israel ((2:4–5) and the northern kingdom (2:6–16)
3. Yahweh condemns Israel’s injustice and religious hypocrisy (3–6)
4. Yahweh warns of coming judgment through visions (7:1–9:10)
5. Yahweh promises restoration and renewal for his people (9:11–15)

### What is the Book of Amos about?

The Book of Amos contains the words of Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa. Amos began to prophesy about 760 BC. He spoke Yahweh’s messages against God’s people behaving wickedly. He spoke messages to both the southern kingdom of Judah and the northern kingdom of Israel.

Yahweh gave Amos prophecies of judgment (Chapters 1–6) to proclaim to the people.

Three visions of Yahweh coming to judge the people are in the last part of the book (7:1–9:10). A final vision promises that Yahweh will restore Israel (9:11–15). He will restore the “tent of David.” This means a descendant of David would once again be king over Israel.

### How should the title of this book be translated?

The traditional title of this book is “The Book of Amos” or just “Amos.” Translators may also call it the “The Book of the Sayings of Amos.”

### Who wrote the Book of Amos?

The prophet Amos probably wrote this book. He lived in the southern kingdom of Judah. Amos came from a poor family. They grew sycamore trees (7:14-15) and were shepherds (1:1). Though Amos was not trained as a prophet, he knew and understood the law of Moses.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### How is justice described in Amos?

Justice is an important theme in the Book of Amos. Justice means people treating others fairly according to the law of Yahweh. People in Israel were oppressing and taking advantage of poor people, orphans, and widows. Amos explained that Yahweh would prefer that the people act justly rather than sacrifice to him. Truly obeying the law of Moses meant being just to other people.

### What is a lawsuit?

Many cultures have a process for resolving disputes through the use of courts. These legal disputes are called lawsuits. Amos uses various legal terms. Part of the book presents events in a courtroom. The people are introduced, the problem is explained, the people are examined, witnesses speak, and a verdict is given.

## Part 3: Important Translation Issues

### What is the meaning of the term “Israel”?

The name “Israel” is used in many different ways in the Bible. Jacob was a son of Isaac. God changed Jacob’s name to Israel. The descendants of Jacob became a nation also called Israel. Eventually, the nation of Israel split into two kingdoms. The northern kingdom was named Israel. The southern kingdom was named Judah. In Amos, “Israel” almost always refers to the northern kingdom of Israel.

### Where do the various narratives begin and end?

The structure of the Book of Amos may make it difficult to understand where Amos ends one thought and begins another. It may be helpful to solve these issues with carefully divided lines or paragraphs.

This traditional Hebrew poetic device continues as in chapter 1 which means complete or overflowing guilt.

# Amos 3 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh holds Israel accountable for rejecting him.

1. Yahweh declares Israel accountable because he chose them (1–2)
2. Yahweh warns of coming judgment and calls his people to listen (3–10)
3. Yahweh announces the destruction of Israel’s wealth and false security (11–15)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The horns of the altar

These projections at the corners of an altar were grasped for refuge; cutting them off (verse 14) means there is no refuge.

### Rhetorical questions

The prophet Amos uses a chain of rhetorical questions to illustrate that God’s judgment on Israel is the expected outcome. Just as everyday causes naturally produce predictable effects, Israel’s persistent sin makes divine disaster an absolute certainty.

Amos is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were the **sons** of their ancestor Israel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [against you Israelites]

Here, **all of the family** represents all of the descendants of those who were captive in Egypt. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of you descendants of those]

Amos first refers to **Yahweh** and then he uses the first person **I** to describe what Yahweh had done. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the second person throughout this verse as in the UST.

The implication is that when Yahweh says that he has **known** Israel, he means that he chose this people to belong to him in a special covenant relationship. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Only you have I chosen to be in a covenant relationship with me]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the nations or people groups that live on the earth. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the people groups that live on the earth]

Yahweh is using **I will visit upon you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will punish you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will punish you for]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [everything you have done wrong]

Yahweh, through Amos, is using the question form to emphasize the certainty of the fact that two people do not travel together unless they have arranged to do so. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Certainly two will not walk together, unless they have agreed!]
The pronoun **they** refers to the two people who agreed to walk together. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [unless the two of them have agreed]

# Amos 4 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh calls Israel to repentance.

1. Yahweh condemns Israel’s oppression and indulgence (1–3)
2. Israel refuses to return to Yahweh despite his warnings (4–11)
3. Yahweh warns Israel to prepare to meet him (12–13)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### “return” to Yahweh

Each disaster in verses 6–11 closes with the refrain “yet you did not return as far as me.” To “return” is to repent and come back to a right relationship with Yahweh.

Amos is speaking to the wealthy women of Samaria, whom he calls **cows of Bashan**, although he knows that they cannot hear him. He is doing this to show his listeners in a strong way how he feels about the way these women oppress the poor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about these women. Alternate translation: [Hear this word about the cows of Bashan]

Amos is speaking of the wealthy women of Samaria as if they were **cows of Bashan**, that is, well-fed cattle grazing in rich pasture on the hillsides overlooking Samaria. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you well-fed, pampered women]

Amos is speaking of the cruel way that these wealthy women are mistreating the needy people as if they were cattle **crushing** them underfoot. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones mistreating the needy]

Amos is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are poor]

Amos is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are needy]

The implication is that the **masters** of these women are their husbands whom they should be serving. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the ones saying to their husbands]
If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [to their masters that they should bring them something to drink]

The women are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Bring drinks to us]

Following the custom of the culture, the Lord Yahweh is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by something sacred, his own **holiness**. Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. Alternate translation: [The Lord Yahweh has solemnly promised, as surely as he is holy]

Amos did not always say who was speaking or who was being addressed. Here, it seems to be the beginning of what Yahweh said but the ULT shows it as Amos telling us what Yahweh said (no quote marks). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark this as a direct quote of Yahweh as in the UST.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by his holy name]
The pronoun **he** refers to their enemies and **you** to the women of Samaria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [when your enemies will lift you women up]

# Amos 5 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. Yahweh mourns Israel’s coming downfall (1–3)
2. Yahweh calls Israel to seek him and reject injustice (4–17)
3. Yahweh warns of the coming day of Yahweh (18–20)
4. Yahweh rejects empty worship and demands justice (21–27)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The gate

Elders decided legal cases at the city gate, so the wrongs in 5:10 and 5:12 are abuses of the courts.

### The day of Yahweh

Israel expected this “day of Yahweh” to bring victory, but it will bring judgment.

# Amos 6 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a woe oracle against Israel’s complacent leaders (verses 1-7) and Yahweh’s sworn judgment (verses 8-14).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Woe

A [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/woe]] announces coming disaster in the tone of a funeral lament.

### Oath

In verse 8 Yahweh swears by his own soul, since there is no one greater. See [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/oath]].

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Chains of participles

The dashes in verses 3-6 and 13 mark phrases describing the people of verse 1.

Quote: הִנְ⁠נִי֩ מֵקִ֨ים עֲלֵי⁠כֶ֜ם בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל נְאֻם־יְהוָ֛ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י הַ⁠צְּבָא֖וֹת גּ֑וֹי וְ⁠לָחֲצ֥וּ אֶתְ⁠כֶ֛ם
Note: The phrase **the declaration of Yahweh, the God of Armies** interrupts what Yahweh is saying, coming between the words **behold me raising up against you, house of Israel** and the words **a nation, and they will oppress you**. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about this declaration before the information about what Yahweh is doing. Alternate translation: [this is the declaration of Yahweh, the God of Armies: behold me raising up a nation against you, house of Israel, and they will oppress you]

Yahweh is using **behold me raising up** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I am about to raise up.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to raise up]

Amos is using **the declaration of Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

In this verse, the word **nation** is singular in form, but it refers to all of the people of that nation as a group. That is why Yahweh then speaks of that nation with the plural pronoun **they**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “nation.” Alternate translation: [people of another nation, and they will oppress you]

Yahweh is referring to all of the land of Israel by naming two extremes, **Lebo Hamath** in the far north and **the brook of the Arabah** in the far south. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [throughout your whole land]

# Amos 7 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is mainly written as a narrative about the prophet Amos interacting with Yahweh. Yahweh presents three different scenarios of judgment before Amos who pleads with God and he does not carry out His judgment. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/judge]])

In the latter part of the chapter, it is important to follow the conversation carefully to understand who is speaking. There are some instances of “reported speech.” (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-quotations]])

# Amos 8 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is written in poetic form and it shows the way Yahweh’s people are sinning and
 how he is going to respond. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/peopleofgod]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “This is the declaration of Yahweh”

This phrase is used to introduce prophecy. It highlights what God is proclaiming. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])

Quote: Look, a basket of summer fruit!
Note: The word “look” here shows that Amos saw something interesting. Alternate translation: [I saw a basket of summer fruit!]
Alternate translation: [ripe fruit]
Yahweh uses a question to teach Amos. Alternate translation: [Tell me what you see, Amos.]

The word translated as **summer fruit** sounds very much like the word for **end**. Yahweh’s purpose in showing Amos summer fruit was to give him a prophecy of the end of his people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.
Alternate translation: [at that time]
This could mean: (1) Yahweh is to telling the people to be silent as they hear about the severity of his punishment or (2) the people will be silent because of their grief after Yahweh’s punishment.
Amos is speaking to the wealthy merchants who harm those who are poor.

Quote: you who trample the needy and remove the poor of the land
Note: This can be restated to remove the nominal adjectives “the needy” and “the poor.” Alternate translation: [you who trample those who are in need and remove those in the land that are poor]
Harming people is spoken of as if it were stomping on people. Alternate translation: [you who harm] or [you who oppress]

Quote: They say, When will the new moon be over, so we can sell grain again? When will the Sabbath day be over, so that we can sell wheat?
Note: The merchants use theses question to emphasize that want to start selling their items again. Alternate translation: [They are always asking when the new moon will be over or when the Sabbath will be over so that can sell their grain and wheat again]

Quote: We will make the measure small and increase the price, as we cheat with false scales
Note: The merchants would use false scales that showed that the amount of grain they were giving was greater than it really was and that the weight of the payment was less than it really was.

Quote: the needy for a pair of sandals
Note: The words “and buy” are understood. Alternate translation: [buy the needy for a pair of sandals]

As in 6:8, **the pride of Jacob** could refer to: (1) the land of Israel, since that is its meaning elsewhere, and it would make no sense to swear by something negative, such as sinful pride. Alternate translation: [by this land that Jacob’s people are so proud of] (2) Yahweh himself. This would then be equivalent to the phrase in 6:8, “The Lord Yahweh has sworn by his soul.” Alternate translation: [by himself, of whom Jacob’s people are so proud]

Quote: Will not the land quake for this, and every one who lives in it mourn?
Note: Amos uses a question to emphasize that these things will certainly happen. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will cause the land to shake, and every one who lives in it will mourn.]

Quote: All of it will rise up like the Nile River … like the river of Egypt
Note: Amos compares the rising and sinking of the waters of the Nile River to how Yahweh will cause the land to shake when he judges the people.
This is another name for the Nile River.

Quote: It will come in that day
Note: Alternate translation: [It will happen at that time]
A person shaves his head to show that he is grieving. Alternate translation: [cause you all to shave your heads]

Quote: like mourning for an only son
Note: It is understood that the only son has died. Alternate translation: [like mourning for an only son who has died]

Quote: a bitter day to its end
Note: Terrible and sad things happening during a day is spoken of as if the day had a bitter taste. Alternate translation: [everything that happens at that time will cause you great sorrow]
This speaks of a future time as if “days are coming.” Alternate translation: [there will be a time] or [in the future]

Note: Yahweh refusing to give messages when the people want to hear from him is spoken of as if there would be a famine of his words. Alternate translation: [when I will cause something like a famine in the land … but for hearing the words of Yahweh]

Note: Here “sea to sea” and “the north to the east” represent all of the land of Israel. Alternate translation: [They will wander here and there and search all over for the word of Yahweh]
This implies the Dead Sea in the south and the Mediterranean Sea in the west.
Alternate translation: [At that time]
to lose all strength

# Amos 9 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is written in poetic form and continues to show the awesome and terrible judgment of Yahweh on his people. In verse 11, the writer writes about the forgiveness and mercy of God on the kingdom of Israel. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/judge]], [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/peopleofgod]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/forgive]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/mercy]])
# General Information:\n\nYahweh shows Amos another vision.
It is uncertain to whom Yahweh is speaking these commands.

Note: It is implied that Yahweh is speaking about the pillars and foundations of a temple.

Note: Here “foundations” represents the whole temple. Alternate translation: [so that the whole temple will shake]

Note: Here “heads” represents the whole person. Alternate translation: [Break the pillars so that the temple falls on all of the people and kills them]

Note: Here “sword” represents an army attacking with their weapons. Alternate translation: [I will send an enemy army to kill the rest of them]

Note: Yahweh uses an exaggerated image of people fleeing to Sheol or heaven to try to escape being killed. Alternate translation: [Even if they were to flee to Sheol or to heaven, they would not be able to escape me]

Note: Here “hand” represents Yahweh’s power. Alternate translation: [I will pull them up from there]

Note: Yahweh gives an exaggerated image of the people fleeing to the top of mount Carmel or to the bottom of the sea to escape being killed. Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Though enemies capture them and force them to go to a foreign land]

Note: Here “sword” represents their enemies. Alternate translation: [there I will cause their enemies to kill them]

Note: Here “eyes” represents seeing. Alternate translation: [I will watch closely and make sure only bad things happen to them and not good things]

Note: Here “the River” and “river of Egypt” both refer to the Nile river. Yahweh causing the land to shake violently is compared to the waters of the Nile river rising and sinking.

Note: These are probably the steps that ancient people imagined led up to God’s palace in the heavens. However, some modern versions wish to read a different Hebrew word meaning “palace” or “rooms.” Here “his steps” probably is a metonym for God’s palace.

Note: Here “vault” refers to the sky which biblical writers described as being a dome over the earth. Alternate translation: [he sets the sky over the earth]

Note: This represents God causing the sea water to fall on the earth as rain. See how you translated this in [Amos 5:8](../05/08.md). Alternate translation: [He takes the waters of the sea and makes them rain down on the surface of the earth]

Note: The idiom “from the face of the earth” means “completely.” Alternate translation: [I will completely destroy this kingdom]

Note: The picture here is of grain falling through the sieve and stones being kept out. The idea is that Yahweh will remove all of the sinful people from Israel.
a surface with many small holes that allow small things to pass through and keep larger things from passing through

The meaning of the word translated as **pebble** could also be translated as “small grain,” and thus it is uncertain whether the grain stays in the sieve or passes through. In either case, the meaning of the comparison is the same; God is using the nations as a sieve to sort out the people of Israel into those who are faithful to him (the grain) and those who are not (the stones). You may want to choose how you translate this comparison depending on whether the grain in your area is bigger or smaller than the holes in a sieve. To summarize, this word could mean: (1) a small stone. In this case, the sieve is retaining the stones and letting the grain fall through, as in the ULT and UST. (2) a small piece of something, such as grain. In this case, the sieve is retaining the grain and letting the small stones fall through. Note: Here “sword” represents their enemies. Alternate translation: [Enemies will kill all the sinners of my people]
